title: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing
question: What protects the things you build with, and how do the four forms of intellectual property differ?
representation: Mixed method. A concept map places one hypothetical app at the centre, with each borrowed component as a spoke. This shows what a project contains and why unknown licences matter. An aligned matrix then compares the four RA 8293 forms on the same criteria: what is protected, how it arises, and how long it lasts. A computing example sits in each row. The text carries the facts. Connector labels are short and the cards are spacious, so nothing overlaps. The example illustrates reasoning and is not a legal verdict.

example.title: Illustrative case: a small team's app
example.description: A hypothetical app uses a library, an image, a font and a copied snippet. Each beat asks what protection or licence might apply to a component. This is not a legal verdict on any real use.

chapters.title: Everything you build borrows
chapters.question: What outside material does a typical project contain?
chapters.insight: Every practitioner uses code, images, fonts, data and text written by other people. Listing each component and its licence, and writing 'unknown' where you cannot tell, makes the gaps countable.
chapters.safeguard: 'Unknown' does not mean 'free to use'. The diagnostic answers are not supplied, so none are given here.
chapters.narration: Start with one small app. It looks like a single product, but it quietly borrows a library, an image, a font and a pasted snippet. Each was written by someone else, so each may carry its own terms. The first professional habit is simple: list every component, write down its licence, and write unknown where you cannot tell. Counting those unknowns shows where to look next, and sets up the later dependency audit.

chapters.title: Four forms of protection under RA 8293
chapters.question: What does each form protect, how does it arise, and how long does it last?
chapters.insight: The four forms differ in what they cover and how they begin. Copyright arises automatically, patent only by grant, trade secret by keeping secrecy, and trademark by registration and use.
chapters.safeguard: Copyright protects expression, not the idea. Reading how a system works and building your own is ordinarily permissible; copying the code is not. For commercially significant projects, ask counsel.
chapters.narration: Philippine law, through the Intellectual Property Code, separates four forms of protection. Read each row across the same columns. Copyright covers expression and arises on creation. A patent covers qualifying inventions and exists only after a grant. A trade secret lasts while information stays confidential. A trademark identifies goods or services. For our app, the code and image fall under copyright, while a logo falls under trademark. This supports comparing the forms in Activity 6.1.

chapters.title: Fair use is weighed, not assumed
chapters.question: What is weighed for fair use, and what do people wrongly assume?
chapters.insight: Fair use is an assessment of several factors together. Credit and educational purpose are inputs or habits to correct, not shortcuts to a lawful result.
chapters.safeguard: The snippet is illustrative only. No factor is scored and no verdict is given. Seek counsel for significant projects.
chapters.narration: Fair use under Philippine law is assessed against several factors: the purpose and character of the use, the nature of the work, the amount used relative to the whole, and the effect on the market. No single factor settles it. Two habits need correcting early. Crediting the author is not permission, and an educational purpose weighs in but is not an exemption. Our snippet stays undecided.

chapters.title: Read the conditions, not the label
chapters.question: What does each licence family permit, require and mean for a product?
chapters.insight: A licence is permission on stated conditions. The same component carries different obligations as its family changes, and copyleft duties attach to distribution.
chapters.safeguard: This summary table is not the full licence text. A checklist cannot establish compliance, and GPL duties attach to distribution, not private use.
chapters.narration: A licence is permission on stated conditions, so read the conditions rather than the label. Public domain dedication permits any use and requires nothing. Permissive licences such as MIT and BSD ask you to retain notice and licence text. Weak copyleft, like LGPL, requires published modifications to the component. Strong copyleft, like GPL, can require the whole distributed work to carry the same terms. A proprietary agreement states its own limits. With no licence stated, nothing is permitted by default.

chapters.title: Walk the licence route
chapters.question: In order, what does each licence family permit and require, from least to most constraining?
chapters.insight: A licence is permission on stated conditions. Walking six fixed stops in order lets you retrieve each family's typical conditions. The order is a memory aid, not a legal ranking.
chapters.safeguard: These are typical conditions only. Real licence text governs, and the checklist alone cannot establish compliance. GPL duties here relate to distribution.
chapters.narration: Imagine walking a route with six stops. Start at an open door, where public domain asks nothing. Next is a stamped notice for permissive licences, which require keeping the notice. Then a shared chain, where weak copyleft requires sharing changes to the component. A locked bundle follows, where strong copyleft can pull the whole distributed work under the same terms. A meter marks proprietary payment and limits. Last is a blank sign, meaning no permission.

roles.stop-public: 1 Open door: public domain: A public domain dedication permits any use and requires nothing. For the app's library, no obligation would follow from the licence.
roles.stop-permissive: 2 Stamped notice: permissive: Permissive licences such as MIT and BSD permit use, modification and distribution, including commercial use. They require keeping the notice and licence text.
roles.stop-weak: 3 Shared chain: weak copyleft: Weak copyleft such as LGPL permits use in a larger work. Modifications to the component must be published. Linking is usually permitted.
roles.stop-strong: 4 Locked bundle: strong copyleft: Strong copyleft such as GPL permits use, modification and distribution. It requires the whole distributed work under the same terms, which can mean publishing your source.
roles.stop-proprietary: 5 Meter: proprietary: Proprietary or commercial licences permit only what the agreement states. They require payment and seat or use limits. Exceeding the limits risks audit exposure.
roles.stop-none: 6 Blank sign: no licence stated: When no licence is stated, nothing is permitted by default. Use is not permitted, so this is not free use.

chapters.title: Open source runs on reciprocity
chapters.question: What three obligations come with taking part in open source?
chapters.insight: Raymond (1999) described a model in which taking part brings three separate obligations. Authority to contribute, honoring conditions and not free-riding each answer a different question.
chapters.safeguard: Making source available is required only where the licence says so. Reciprocity is the described model, not a universal legal rule. No ownership decision follows from these facts.
chapters.narration: Open collaboration works on reciprocity, as Raymond described in 1999. Taking part brings three obligations. First, you need the right to contribute, which depends on your employment agreement. Second, honor the licences you incorporate by retaining notices and, where the licence requires it, making source available. Third, don't free-ride, because using others' work without honoring its conditions breaks the commons that everyone depends on.

chapters.title: Who owns what you write at work
chapters.question: How do the IP Code and your employment agreement together decide ownership?
chapters.insight: The source says ownership is governed by the IP Code and the employment agreement, read together. Employment agreements commonly assign work, so the clause's wording matters more than a general rule.
chapters.safeguard: Employment agreements commonly assign work, but this does not mean the employer always owns side projects or never does. The outcome depends on the clause, which you must read.
chapters.narration: Start with the document that assigns work. Ownership is governed by the IP Code and your employment agreement read together, so first find the assigning clause. Then check its reach. It may cover only work made in the course of employment, or anything made during the whole employment period. If a side project matters, ask for a written carve-out. Finally, keep personal work on your own time and equipment. None of this decides ownership alone, because the wording does.

roles.read-clause: 1. Read the clause: Before signing, find the clause that assigns work to the employer. An assignment clause transfers ownership of what you create. Your side projects, thesis code and open source contributions may all be affected.
roles.check-reach: 2. Check its reach: The clause may cover only work made in the course of employment, or anything made during the whole employment period. For example, a weekend app could fall inside the wider wording but outside the narrower one.
roles.ask-carveout: 3. Ask for a carve-out: A carve-out is a written exception that excludes named work from the clause. If a side project matters to you, request an exception in writing instead of assuming one exists.
roles.keep-separate: 4. Keep work separate: Do personal work on your own time and your own equipment. This keeps your personal work distinct from your job, but the agreement's wording still decides who owns it.

documentTitle: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing

sources.title: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing

checks.evidence: The beat applies the Explore task (list each external component with its licence or 'unknown', count the unknowns, keep the list for Activity 6.3) and the page 1 point that practitioners use others' code, images, fonts, data and text. The hypothetical app is an illustrative device, and 'unknown does not mean free to use' is a fair inference from the page 6 row 'No licence stated: nothing by default'.

The beat matches Table 6.1 on what each form protects, how it arises and how long it lasts (life plus fifty years, twenty years from filing, indefinite until disclosed, renewable indefinitely). The copyright and trademark examples (code and images, name and logo), the 'expression, not ideas' safeguard and the Activity 6.1 link all follow pages 4 and 10.

The four factors (purpose and character, nature of the work, amount used relative to the whole, effect on the market) and the statements that no single factor settles fair use, that attribution is not permission and that education is not an exemption all match page 5. The snippet is hypothetical and is left undecided, so no verdict is asserted.

The permits, requires and consequence cells for public domain, MIT/BSD, LGPL, GPL, proprietary and no-licence match Table 6.2 on page 6. 'Can require' is kept for GPL, and 'nothing permitted by default' for no licence. The remark that GPL duties attach to distribution is a reasonable inference from 'whole distributed work' and is extra background, not a contradiction of the source.

The six licence families, their permissions, requirements and consequences match Table 6.2. Examples include 'GPL can require publishing your source', 'linking usually permitted', and 'no licence stated means nothing is permitted by default'. The safeguards (typical conditions only, GPL duties relate to distribution, order is a memory aid) are qualifications, not contradictions.

The three obligations (right to contribute depends on the employment agreement, honor incorporated licences by retaining notices and making source available where the licence requires it, don't free-ride) match page 7, including the Raymond (1999) attribution. The 'model, not law' framing and the practical advice to check the agreement before contributing are fair applications, not invented facts.

The lesson follows page 8: ownership is governed by the IP Code and the employment agreement read together, the clause may cover work made in the course of employment or anything made during the employment period, a carve-out is requested in writing, and personal work is kept on your own time and equipment. Page 9 supports that agreements commonly assign work. The lesson also says the agreement's wording still decides ownership, so it does not claim that personal equipment guarantees ownership.

The lesson matches the pages: Activity 6.3 audits components, licences, obligations and compliance status, and attribution is not permission. Code with no licence conveys no permission. Licence families differ in what they require. The steps for the snippet (verify the licence, seek permission or replace it, ask counsel) are practical applications that promise no outcome. The lesson says that Case 5, the answer keys and the rubrics are not supplied, which is accurate because the PDF only references them.

storyboard.title: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing
storyboard.question: What protects the things you build with, what does each licence actually let you do and require, and who owns what you write at work?
storyboard.representation: Mixed method. Matrix (aligned conditions) for the four IP forms and the licence families, so the criteria are explicit and comparable. Concept map around one worked case for fair use and reciprocity. Process for the employment-ownership steps. Loci route (stable landmarks, same order) only for recall of the licence spectrum, from 'no obligation' to 'no permission'. Cue mappings: open door → public domain; stamped notice → permissive (retain notice); shared chain → weak copyleft; locked-together bundle → GPL; meter/ticket → proprietary; blank sign → no licence. Cues aid recall of order; the table text carries the facts. The recall check is a proposal and depends on renderer support.

example.title: Illustrative case: a small team's app and one borrowed component
example.description: Track one hypothetical app that uses a library, an image and a copied snippet. Each beat asks what applies to that component. The case is illustrative, not a legal verdict on any real use.

beats.title: Everything you build borrows
beats.question: What outside material does a typical project contain?
beats.insight: Projects contain code, images, fonts, data and text made by others. The module aims to keep a graduate out of legal trouble. Start by inventorying components and their licences, and mark unknowns.
beats.visibleOperation: Before: the app alone. Change: library, image, font, snippet and dataset connect to it, each with a licence tag that reads 'unknown' until resolved. After: the unknowns are countable. This sets up the audit in Activity 6.3.
beats.safeguard: Avoid reading 'unknown' as 'free to use'. The module treats unlicensed use as not permitted. Diagnostic questions on Modules 1–5 are not answered, because Appendix A is not supplied.

beats.title: Four forms of protection under RA 8293
beats.question: What does each form protect, how does it arise, and how long does it last?
beats.insight: Copyright covers expression and arises automatically (life of the author plus fifty years). Patent covers inventions by grant (twenty years from filing). Trade secret depends on secrecy (indefinite until disclosed). Trademark arises by registration and use (renewable).
beats.visibleOperation: Before: an empty grid of 4 forms by 4 criteria plus a computing example. Change: rows fill in order, and the case components are placed in the matching row. After: the learner compares forms across the same criteria. This supports Activity 6.1 and the ILO 6.1 comparison.
beats.safeguard: Avoid confusing copyright's protection of expression with protection of the idea. Say that learning how a system works and building your own is ordinarily permissible, and copying the code is not.

beats.title: Fair use is weighed, not assumed
beats.question: What do we weigh, and what do people wrongly assume?
beats.insight: Four factors are assessed together: purpose and character, nature of the work, amount used, and market effect. None settles the matter. Attribution is not permission, and education is not an exemption.
beats.visibleOperation: Before: the copied snippet beside a scale. Change: four factor objects connect to the scale, then 'credit given' and 'educational' are attached without tipping it to 'lawful'. After: they are inputs, not verdicts. The Boyle point warns against assuming either extreme.
beats.safeguard: Avoid showing any numeric weighting or a verdict. Use no 'fair'/'unfair' result for the snippet. It is illustrative only, with counsel for significant projects.

beats.title: Read the conditions, not the label
beats.question: What does each licence family permit, require and mean for a product?
beats.insight: Public domain: any use, nothing required. MIT/BSD: retain notice and licence text. LGPL: modifications to the component published. GPL: the whole distributed work under the same terms. Proprietary: the agreement's limits. No licence: nothing by default.
beats.visibleOperation: Before: six family rows with the Permits column visible. Change: Requires and Consequence columns reveal, and the case library slides along the rows. After: the learner can see how the same component changes the obligations as its family changes. This supports ILO 6.2.
beats.safeguard: Preserve qualifiers: LGPL linking is 'usually permitted', and GPL 'can require' publishing source. GPL obligations attach to distribution, not private use. Do not treat the summary table as the full licence text.

beats.title: Walk the licence route
beats.question: In order, what does each landmark require, from least to most constraining?
beats.insight: A fixed route of six landmarks stores the order of the families as a recall aid. Retrieval matters more than viewing, so the learner retraces the route and states each requirement before the reveal.
beats.visibleOperation: Before: the route with labeled landmarks. Change: the cue's text hides, the learner steps through the stops, and the requirement reveals on selection. After: the learner has retrieved all six in place. Use route and shield or key icons only as cues for the facts.
beats.safeguard: Avoid reading the route order as a legal ranking. The cues cover the families' typical conditions only. A 'blank sign' means no permission, not free use. Do not claim any recall gain.

beats.title: Open source runs on reciprocity
beats.question: What three obligations come with taking part in open source?
beats.insight: Raymond (1999) describes the model. First, you need the right to contribute, which is a question about your employment agreement. Second, honor incorporated licences by keeping notices and, where required, making source available. Third, don't free-ride.
beats.visibleOperation: Before: a contributor and a shared repository. Change: three labeled links trace between them, each tied to its condition. After: the learner sees that contributing, using and honoring conditions are separate obligations.
beats.safeguard: Avoid reading 'make source available' as always required. It applies where the licence requires it. Avoid treating reciprocity as a legal rule when it is the described model.

beats.title: Who owns what you write at work
beats.question: How do the IP Code and your employment agreement together decide ownership?
beats.insight: Read the assigning clause before signing. Check its reach: it may cover work made in the course of employment, or anything made during the employment period. Ask for a written carve-out if a side project matters. Keep personal work on your own time and equipment.
beats.visibleOperation: Before: a person, an employer and a side project. Change: four steps trace in order and the clause's reach widens from course-of-employment work to the whole period. After: the learner knows when the clause matters. Ownership turns on the actual agreement.
beats.safeguard: Avoid concluding that the employer always owns side projects, or never does. Agreements 'commonly' assign work. The outcome depends on the clause, which the learner must read.

beats.title: Apply it: audit and assess
beats.question: How do you audit a project and answer the assessment items?
beats.insight: Summary: copyright is automatic, patents are granted, attribution is not permission, and no licence means no permission. The audit lists each component, licence, obligation and status, and notes how AI-assistant code was treated.
beats.visibleOperation: Before: the case's component list with unknowns. Change: each is resolved or flagged, and the learner picks answers to the Part A items and the unlicensed-snippet scenario. After: a status list and an action plan. Case 5 in Appendix C.2 is not supplied, so it cannot be answered.
beats.safeguard: Avoid inventing Case 5, Appendix A keys or rubrics. State they are missing. Frame the snippet advice as steps (stop, verify the licence, seek permission or replace, ask counsel), not a guaranteed outcome.

In 'four-forms', the matrix layout cleanly presents the four RA 8293 protection forms across four well-aligned columns with distinct icons, clean row card framing, and accurate source fidelity.

The concept layout for 'fair-use-weighed' cleanly maps the four statutory fair use factors and two common habits to correct around the illustrative copied snippet with distinct color coding, legible typography, and clear relational connector labels.

The matrix layout for 'licence-families' neatly structures all six licence tiers across aligned columns detailing permissions, requirements, and product implications with excellent contrast and no clipping.

In reciprocity, the four-stage horizontal process layout renders cleanly with well-aligned cards, distinct icons, labeled connector arrows ('precedes', 'avoids free-riding', 'sustains'), and complete explanatory text.

narrationScript: Start with one small app. It looks like a single product, but it quietly borrows a library, an image, a font and a pasted snippet. Each was written by someone else, so each may carry its own terms. The first professional habit is simple: list every component, write down its licence, and write unknown where you cannot tell. Counting those unknowns shows where to look next, and sets up the later dependency audit. Philippine law, through the Intellectual Property Code, separates four forms of protection. Read each row across the same columns. Copyright covers expression and arises on creation. A patent covers qualifying inventions and exists only after a grant. A trade secret lasts while information stays confidential. A trademark identifies goods or services. For our app, the code and image fall under copyright, while a logo falls under trademark. This supports comparing the forms in Activity 6.1. Fair use under Philippine law is assessed against several factors: the purpose and character of the use, the nature of the work, the amount used relative to the whole, and the effect on the market. No single factor settles it. Two habits need correcting early. Crediting the author is not permission, and an educational purpose weighs in but is not an exemption. Our snippet stays undecided. A licence is permission on stated conditions, so read the conditions rather than the label. Public domain dedication permits any use and requires nothing. Permissive licences such as MIT and BSD ask you to retain notice and licence text. Weak copyleft, like LGPL, requires published modifications to the component. Strong copyleft, like GPL, can require the whole distributed work to carry the same terms. A proprietary agreement states its own limits. With no licence stated, nothing is permitted by default. Imagine walking a route with six stops. Start at an open door, where public domain asks nothing. Next is a stamped notice for permissive licences, which require keeping the notice. Then a shared chain, where weak copyleft requires sharing changes to the component. A locked bundle follows, where strong copyleft can pull the whole distributed work under the same terms. A meter marks proprietary payment and limits. Last is a blank sign, meaning no permission. Open collaboration works on reciprocity, as Raymond described in 1999. Taking part brings three obligations. First, you need the right to contribute, which depends on your employment agreement. Second, honor the licences you incorporate by retaining notices and, where the licence requires it, making source available. Third, don't free-ride, because using others' work without honoring its conditions breaks the commons that everyone depends on. Start with the document that assigns work. Ownership is governed by the IP Code and your employment agreement read together, so first find the assigning clause. Then check its reach. It may cover only work made in the course of employment, or anything made during the whole employment period. If a side project matters, ask for a written carve-out. Finally, keep personal work on your own time and equipment. None of this decides ownership alone, because the wording does. Treat the app as the centre of an audit. Each component gets a row: what it is, which licence applies, what that licence requires, and whether you comply. Remember that attribution is not permission, and that code with no licence conveys no permission. So the copied snippet stays flagged as unresolved. Verify its licence, seek permission or replace it, and ask counsel. Case 5 and the answer keys are not supplied, so we cannot answer those items.
